book.title: Calculus II
book.subtitle: From integration techniques to infinite approximation
book.author: AI University · AI-generated
book.description: A complete next course in single-variable calculus: integration methods and errors, improper integrals, sequences and series, Taylor expansions, parametric and polar curves, and introductory first-order differential equations.
book.audience: Learners familiar with Calculus I limits, derivatives, definite integrals and substitution
book.scope: Eight complete chapters, including geometric and physical integral models, introductory first-order equations and numerical methods. Multivariable calculus, higher-order equations, complex series and full real analysis belong to separate volumes.

chapters.title: Integration techniques
chapters.subtitle: Rewrite unfamiliar integrals in familiar forms
chapters.intro: Simplify first, then choose substitution, parts, identities or partial fractions. Check results by differentiation or recombining fractions.

chapters.title: Approximating, extending and modeling integrals
chapters.subtitle: Improper integrals and geometric and physical applications
chapters.intro: Numerical methods address accuracy; improper integrals address limiting existence. Surface area, centers of mass and pressure each require their own small-piece model.
goals: Model area, center of mass and force

chapters.title: From sequences to infinite sums
chapters.subtitle: Sequence limits and infinite summation
chapters.intro: Sequence limits underpin series. First examine later terms, then determine whether their running totals stabilize.

chapters.title: Series convergence and error
chapters.subtitle: Every convergence test has hypotheses
chapters.intro: Start with the term test, then choose according to positivity, ratios or alternation. Convergence, exact sums and error estimates are distinct questions.
goals: Choose comparison, integral, ratio or root tests

chapters.title: From convergence to function representation
chapters.subtitle: Changing the input changes the series
chapters.intro: Distinguish absolute and conditional convergence, treat inputs as parameters, and develop power series, termwise operations and Taylor polynomials.

chapters.title: Taylor expansions in calculation
chapters.subtitle: Approximations need ranges and error bounds
chapters.intro: Use remainders to control errors, transform basic expansions, and apply them to nonelementary integrals, limits and radical approximations.
goals: Use series for integrals and limits

chapters.title: Parametric curves and polar coordinates
chapters.subtitle: Describe how a point traces a curve
chapters.intro: Parameters determine position, direction and repetitions. Check tracing ranges before computing tangents, arc lengths or sector areas.
goals: Handle polar coordinates and swept areas

chapters.title: First-order differential equations
chapters.subtitle: From local change to entire trajectories
chapters.intro: Use initial values to select solutions and check equilibria and intervals. Separation and integrating factors give analytic solutions; Euler supplies discrete approximations for comparison.

questions.problem: Find $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\tan x-x}{x^3}$.

questions.problem: For $y\prime=y,y(0)=2$ with $h=0.2$, compute two Euler steps.

glossary.term: Mass, moments and center of mass
glossary.meaning: The center of mass is a mass-weighted average, not a simple average of boundary positions.
Total force and work accumulate layer contributions; force or travel distance can differ between layers.
A sequence converges when every sufficiently late term stays close to one number. Finitely many initial terms do not determine its limit.
A bounded monotone real sequence converges. Pass a recurrence to its limit only after proving convergence.
A series converges when its partial sums converge. Terms tending to zero are necessary, not sufficient.
Find finite partial sums before taking a limit. Do not manipulate an infinite expression whose convergence is unknown.

glossary.term: The integral test and tail bounds
glossary.meaning: A positive, continuous, decreasing function links an integral to a series and bounds the tail after a finite partial sum.
Compare positive terms with a known series. Limit comparison checks whether their tails differ by a finite positive factor.
A limiting consecutive ratio or nth root below one gives a convergent geometric bound. A limit equal to one is inconclusive.
An alternating series with eventually nonincreasing positive magnitudes tending to zero converges. Once truncation enters that decreasing tail, its error is at most the next magnitude.
Absolute convergence means the absolute-value series converges. Conditional convergence means the original series converges but its absolute-value series diverges.
A power series converges inside its radius and diverges outside. Test each boundary point separately.
Inside the convergence interval, power series can be differentiated and integrated term by term. The radius stays the same; endpoints may change.
A Taylor polynomial matches the value and first few derivatives at its center. This local agreement does not guarantee accuracy far away.
A Taylor polynomial gives an approximation; a bound on the next derivative limits its error.
Exponential, sine, cosine, geometric and logarithmic expansions generate many others by substitution and calculus. Keep each convergence range.

glossary.term: Using series for integrals and limits
glossary.meaning: Series approximate integrals without elementary antiderivatives and reveal the first surviving term in a limit.
Binomial coefficients extend to any real exponent. Nonnegative integer exponents terminate; others generally yield infinite series with limited convergence ranges.
Parametric equations specify how a point moves. The same geometric curve can have different directions and speeds.

glossary.term: Tangents and arc length of parametric curves
glossary.meaning: Parametric slope is vertical rate divided by horizontal rate. Arc length accumulates speed.
Polar coordinates give radius and angle. A negative radius moves opposite the stated direction.
Polar area accumulates small sectors, while arc length accumulates short arcs. Check tracing ranges to avoid repetition.
A differential equation specifies slope; an initial value specifies a starting point. A direction field shows the local directions allowed.
If a rate factors into a function of each variable, separate and integrate. Find equilibria before dividing by the dependent-variable factor.
For $y\prime+p(x)y=q(x)$, multiply by a suitable function to combine the left side into one product derivative.

glossary.term: Euler's method and the logistic model
glossary.meaning: Euler advances using the current slope. Logistic growth slows as remaining capacity decreases.

appendices.title: Why Taylor's theorem uses an intermediate point
appendices.text: Fix the target $x\neq a$. Write $F(t)=f(t)-T_m(t)-K(t-a)^{m+1}$, choosing $K$ so that $F(x)=0$. The function and its first $m$ derivatives vanish at the center. Repeated Rolle applications yield an intermediate point $\xi$ with $F^{(m+1)}(\xi)=0$, hence $K=\frac{f^{(m+1)}(\xi)}{(m+1)!}$. This gives the remainder formula. Handle endpoint or zero-distance cases by continuity or direct equality.

appendices.title: Power-series endpoints and Abel's continuity theorem
appendices.text: If $\sum c_n$ converges, Abel's theorem gives $\lim_{r\to1^-}\sum c_nr^n=\sum c_n$. This links an interior function representation to a convergent endpoint; the theorem is cited, not fully proved here. Finite geometric sums and summation by parts control tails. Endpoint convergence alone does not replace the linking argument. This result identifies logarithm at 1 and arctangent at plus or minus one.

appendices.title: Why the generalized binomial series represents the function
appendices.text: For a nonterminating series, the ratio test proves convergence on $|x|<1$. Termwise differentiation inside the interval and the coefficient recurrence show its sum $S$ satisfies $(1+x)S\prime=\alpha S$, $S(0)=1$. The function $(1+x)^\alpha$ solves the same initial-value problem. Continuous coefficients and first-order linear uniqueness make them equal. The ratio test alone establishes convergence, not the sum's identity.

appendices.title: The scope of differential-equation existence and uniqueness
appendices.text: Continuity of the right side and its vertical partial derivative near the initial point gives a unique local solution. This theorem is cited, not fully proved here. Local uniqueness does not guarantee existence on the entire real axis: $y\prime=y^2$, $y(0)=1$ blows up at a finite time. Higher-order equations, systems, rigorous numerical stability and full existence theory belong to the differential-equations volumes.

body.title: Which factor should be differentiated?
body.text: Try differentiating a polynomial or logarithm. Check whether the new integral is actually simpler.

body.title: When is repetition useful?
body.text: For a polynomial times an exponential, repeat until the polynomial disappears. If the original integral returns, solve for it algebraically.

body.text: Evaluate the boundary term at both endpoints. For an infinite limit, first truncate the interval, then take a limit.

commonMistakes.correction: If the new integral is harder, swap the choices. Judge the method by what remains.

lessons.subtitle: Use identities to expose a substitution
lessons.concept: For odd powers, reserve a derivative factor; for even powers, use power-reduction identities.
lessons.intuition: In $\sin^3x$, reserve $\sin x$ and replace the remaining $\sin^2x$ with $1-\cos^2x$.

body.title: Products of sine and cosine
body.text: For odd sine powers, reserve one sine and set $u=\cos x$; reverse the roles for odd cosine powers. If both powers are even, use half-angle identities.

body.title: Powers of tangent and secant
body.text: In $\tan^m x\sec^n x$ with nonnegative integer powers, if $n\ge2$ is even, reserve $\sec^2x\,dx$ and set $u=\tan x$. If $m\ge1$ is odd and $n\ge1$, reserve $\sec x\tan x\,dx$ and set $u=\sec x$. Other cases require another identity or integration by parts.

body.title: Check the interval
body.text: Formulas involving $\tan x$ or $\sec x$ apply on intervals avoiding $\cos x=0$. Differentiate to check signs.

formalDefinition.text: Use identities to expose a substitution
conditions: Angles are in radians. Transform the differential along with the variable.

derivation.text: Split the odd power.

Integrate the resulting polynomial.

lessons.title: Trigonometric substitution
lessons.subtitle: Use identities to simplify square roots
lessons.concept: Match the substitution to the radical, then choose an angle interval to handle absolute values correctly.
lessons.intuition: $x=a\sin\theta$ turns $\sqrt{a^2-x^2}$ into $a|\cos\theta|$. On $-\frac\pi2\leq\theta\leq\frac\pi2$, cosine is nonnegative.

body.title: Which substitution fits?
body.text: For $a^2-x^2$ use sine; for $a^2+x^2$ use tangent; for $x^2-a^2$ use secant on the $x\geq a$ branch, where $a>0$.

body.title: Why draw a triangle?
body.text: A triangle converts trigonometric ratios back to the original variable. It describes one branch, not every possible sign.

body.title: What else changes?
body.text: The differential $dx$ changes too. A denominator's radical often cancels a factor from the differential.

steps: Write $A/x+(Bx+C)/(x^2+1)$. Match coefficients in $2x+3=(A+B)x^2+Cx+A$ to obtain $A=3,B=-3,C=2$.
Integrate $3/x-3x/(x^2+1)+2/(x^2+1)$ term by term. Use $u=x^2+1$ for the second term and arctangent for the third.
$x^2+1>0$; the only pole is $x=0$. Choose integration constants separately on the positive and negative half-lines.

commonMistakes.claim: Only the highest repeated power is needed.
commonMistakes.correction: Lower-power terms generally must also be included.

commonMistakes.claim: For a denominator factor $x^2+1$, use only a constant numerator.
commonMistakes.correction: Use $Ax+B$ in general; either coefficient may turn out to be zero.

practice.hint: Factor the denominator as a difference of squares.
solution: Write $\frac A{x-1}+\frac B{x+1}$; substituting $x=1,-1$ gives $A=\frac12,B=-\frac12$.

practice.hint: Evaluate the logarithm at both endpoints.
solution: $[\ln x-\ln(x+1)]_1^2=\ln\frac23-\ln\frac12=\ln\frac43$.
$\frac{x^2}{x^2+1}=1-\frac1{x^2+1}$; integrate term by term.

practice.problem: Write the decomposition form for $\frac1{(x-1)^2(x^2+1)}$, without finding coefficients.
practice.hint: Treat the repeated root and irreducible quadratic separately.
solution: Keep both linear-factor powers; the quadratic's numerator has lower degree.

learningCheck.question: How many fraction terms correspond to the factor $(x-2)^3$?
learningCheck.explanation: Include powers one through three, not just the highest.

teaching.explain: Decomposition preserves the function while making integration easier. Combining denominators determines the coefficients.

lessons.title: Choosing an integration method
lessons.subtitle: Read the structure before choosing a tool
lessons.concept: Simplify and look for an inner derivative, then examine products, radicals or rational functions. A definite integral can exist without an elementary antiderivative.
lessons.intuition: Although both contain exponentials, $\int2xe^{x^2}dx$ suggests substitution and $\int xe^x dx$ suggests parts. Look for the inner derivative outside.

body.title: What should you try first?
body.text: Simplify algebraically, use identities or perform polynomial division. The result may fit a basic formula.

body.title: Can methods be combined?
body.text: Yes. Integration by parts may lead to substitution; a trigonometric substitution may lead to a trigonometric integral. Each step should reduce some difficulty.

body.title: When should you stop seeking an elementary formula?
body.text: Functions such as $e^{-x^2}$ have no elementary antiderivative. Keep the definite integral and use numerical methods or series with an error estimate.

formalDefinition.text: Read the structure before choosing a tool
conditions: The fundamental theorem applies when $f$ is continuous on a finite closed interval; elementary formulas are not required for integrability.

derivation.text: Identify the composite structure first.
The other product calls for integration by parts.
Check every candidate antiderivative by differentiating.

workedExamples.title: Expansion is shorter
steps: Integrate term by term; parts is unnecessary.

workedExamples.title: Combining two methods
steps: Then integration by parts gives $\frac12(u\ln u-u)+C$.

commonMistakes.claim: Each problem must use only one method.
commonMistakes.correction: When the structure changes, switch tools and verify each step.

commonMistakes.claim: Without an elementary antiderivative, the integral cannot exist.
commonMistakes.correction: Continuity guarantees a definite integral on a finite closed interval.

practice.problem: Which method should you try first for $\int\frac{2x}{1+x^2}dx$?
practice.hint: The numerator is the denominator's derivative.
solution: $du=2x dx$; the integral becomes $\int\frac1u du$.

practice.problem: Which method should you try first for $\int x\sin x dx$?
practice.answer: Integration by parts, giving $-x\cos x+\sin x+C$.
solution: $u=x,v=-\cos x$; the remaining integral is $\int\cos x dx$.
$\frac{x^2+1}{x+1}=x-1+\frac2{x+1}$; evaluate the resulting integrals at the endpoints.

practice.problem: Can $\int_0^1e^{-x^2}dx$ be defined despite having no elementary antiderivative?
practice.answer: Yes; its value lies between 0 and 1.
practice.hint: Check continuity on the finite interval first.
solution: The integrand is continuous and satisfies $0<e^{-x^2}\leq1$. The integral exists and can be approximated with error control.

learningCheck.question: Which step should come first?
choices: Use parts whenever a product appears
Simplify and look for a composite structure
learningCheck.explanation: Choose a method from the simplified structure, not just its appearance.

teaching.explain: Ask which rewrite simplifies the next step. Then differentiate your proposed answer to check it.

steps.title: Short interval
steps.observation: The area is $1-\frac12e^{1/2}$; the integration-by-parts expression agrees.

steps.title: Check the endpoint
steps.observation: The integral is 1, as is the boundary term minus the remaining integral.

steps.title: Extend the interval
steps.observation: The integral is $e^2+1$; evaluate both terms on the right.

interactiveVisual.caption: Compare $\int_0^b xe^x dx$ with its boundary term and remaining integral.
interactiveVisual.prediction: As the upper endpoint increases, do both expressions give the same accumulated value?

Combine integration techniques
Distinguish elementary antiderivatives from integrability

lessons.title: Numerical integration and error
lessons.subtitle: Approximate an integral with an error bound
lessons.concept: Trapezoids use straight lines; Simpson's rule uses parabolas. Error bounds tell you how many subintervals suffice.
lessons.intuition: Finer partitions often improve accuracy, but a close-looking graph gives no guarantee. Derivative bounds supply that guarantee.

body.title: Simpson's weights
body.text: Use equal spacing and an even $n$. Endpoints have weight 1; interior odd-indexed nodes have weight 4 and even-indexed nodes weight 2.

body.title: Why do the error bounds differ?
body.text: The trapezoidal bound scales with $n^{-2}$. With a bounded fourth derivative, Simpson's bound scales with $n^{-4}$. Higher-order guarantees require more smoothness.

body.title: Choosing the partition
body.text: Specify a tolerance, insert a derivative bound and solve for a sufficient $n$. The actual error may be smaller than this conservative bound.

formalDefinition.text: Approximate an integral with an error bound
conditions: For trapezoids require $f\in C^2[a,b]$ and $|f^{(2)}|\leq M_2$; for Simpson require $f\in C^4[a,b]$ and $|f^{(4)}|\leq M_4$, with positive even $n$.

derivation.text: Approximate each pair of subintervals with a parabola.
Add the pairs; interior even-indexed nodes occur twice.
Insert a fourth-derivative bound to bound the error.

workedExamples.title: Exact for a quadratic
workedExamples.problem: Use Simpson's rule with two subintervals for $\int_0^1x^2dx$.

workedExamples.title: Choosing the number of subintervals
workedExamples.problem: Approximate $\int_0^1e^x dx$ by trapezoids with error below $0.001$. Give a sufficient number of subintervals.
steps: $M_2=e$, so the error is at most $\frac e{12n^2}$.
workedExamples.answer: Choose 16 subintervals; the bound guarantees the tolerance.

commonMistakes.claim: Simpson's rule permits any odd number of subintervals.
commonMistakes.correction: This composite rule groups subintervals in pairs and requires an even count.

commonMistakes.claim: Two close approximations prove that the error is small.
commonMistakes.correction: Agreement is a diagnostic; a guarantee still needs the hypotheses and an error bound.

practice.hint: Use half weight at the endpoints and full weight internally.
solution: $T_2=\frac14(0+2\cdot\frac14+1)=\frac38$.

practice.problem: What does two-subinterval Simpson give for $\int_0^1x^3dx$?
practice.hint: It is exact for cubics too.
solution: $S_2=\frac16(0+4\cdot\frac18+1)=\frac14$.

practice.problem: The trapezoidal bound uses $M_2=12$ on an interval of length 1. What is the smallest count guaranteeing error at most $0.01$?
solution: $\frac1{n^2}\leq0.01$ gives $n\geq10$.

practice.problem: Can the fourth-derivative bound be used directly when the graph has a corner?
solution: The fourth derivative may not exist. Split at the corner or use an applicable estimate.

learningCheck.question: Composite Simpson's rule requires which number of subintervals?
learningCheck.explanation: Fit a parabola to each pair; interior weights depend on the node's parity.

teaching.explain: The algorithm supplies a number; error theory supplies a guaranteed range. Keep them separate.

steps.title: Two subintervals
steps.observation: Simpson uses a three-point parabola; trapezoids use two line segments.

steps.title: Eight subintervals
steps.observation: For this smooth exponential model, both errors decrease.

steps.title: Thirty-two subintervals
steps.observation: Actual errors and conservative bounds are displayed separately.

interactiveVisual.prediction: With the same partition, which method has the smaller error?

Check even counts and smoothness
Choose sufficient counts for a tolerance

lessons.title: Integrals over infinite intervals
lessons.subtitle: Truncate first, then move the boundary outward
lessons.concept: An infinite-interval integral is a limit of finite integrals. Infinity is not an ordinary endpoint value.
lessons.intuition: A region may extend forever yet have finite area. The tail's rate of decay decides.

body.title: What does convergence mean?
body.text: The integral $\int_a^R f$ must tend to a finite real number as $R\to\infty$. Unbounded growth and persistent oscillation both mean divergence.

body.title: What if both endpoints are infinite?
body.text: Split at a finite point; both halves must converge separately. Symmetric truncation alone may produce only a principal value.

body.title: The power-tail threshold
body.text: On $[1,\infty)$, $\int x^{-p}dx$ converges exactly when $p>1$. Even the slow logarithmic growth at $p=1$ is unbounded.

formalDefinition.text: Truncate first, then move the boundary outward
conditions: Each finite truncation is integrable and the limiting value must be finite. For two infinite endpoints, both halves must converge.

derivation.text: Evaluate a finite truncation.
A negative exponent makes the far-end term vanish.
Check the threshold separately.

workedExamples.title: A finite tail area
steps: As $R\to\infty$, the tail $\frac1R$ tends to zero.

workedExamples.title: An exponential tail
steps: The exponential tends to zero, leaving a finite limit.

commonMistakes.claim: If the function tends to zero, its integral converges.
commonMistakes.correction: $\frac1x\to0$, but its integral from 1 to infinity diverges.

commonMistakes.claim: The two infinite tails can cancel.
commonMistakes.correction: Ordinary improper integration requires each half to converge. Principal value uses a different definition.

practice.hint: Use a finite upper endpoint first.

solution: $2(\sqrt R-1)\to\infty$.

practice.hint: Integrate by parts before taking the limit.
solution: An antiderivative is $-(x+1)e^{-x}$; the truncated value is $1-(R+1)e^{-R}\to1$.

practice.answer: No; the ordinary improper integral diverges.
solution: The integral from 0 to $R$ is $\frac{R^2}{2}\to\infty$. A zero symmetric principal value does not establish convergence.

learningCheck.question: Does $f(x)\to0$ guarantee that $\int_1^\infty f(x)dx$ converges?
learningCheck.explanation: $f(x)=\frac1x$ is a positive counterexample.

teaching.explain: Infinite length need not mean infinite area. Track finite truncations and ask whether their values approach a finite limit.

steps.title: A convergent tail
steps.instruction: Set the exponent to 2 and upper endpoint to 4.
steps.observation: The truncated area is $\frac34$, still $\frac14$ below its limit 1.

steps.title: Move the boundary outward
steps.instruction: Set the exponent to 2 and upper endpoint to 40.
steps.observation: The area is $\frac{39}{40}$; the remaining tail is $\frac1{40}$.

steps.title: The threshold exponent
steps.instruction: Set the exponent to 1 and upper endpoint to 40.
steps.observation: The area is $\ln40$; increasing the endpoint produces no finite limit.

interactiveVisual.prediction: How does extending the interval differ on either side of exponent one?

objectives: Define infinite-interval integrals by truncation limits
Determine convergence of power tails
Distinguish improper integrals from principal values

lessons.title: Unbounded integrands on finite intervals
lessons.subtitle: Approach every singularity separately
lessons.concept: Avoid an unbounded endpoint or interior point, integrate on a truncated interval, then take one-sided limits.
lessons.intuition: Infinite height near zero need not give infinite area. Both height and width matter.

body.title: An interior singularity
body.text: Split at the singularity; both sides must converge. Never subtract antiderivative values across a singularity directly.

body.title: Is the power threshold the same as at infinity?
body.text: It is reversed: $\int_0^1x^{-p}dx$ converges exactly when $p<1$. Here the issue is a spike near zero, not a distant tail.

body.title: Can comparison help?
body.text: Yes. A nonnegative function bounded above by an integrable spike is integrable. One bounded below by a divergent spike diverges.

formalDefinition.text: Approach every singularity separately
conditions: Truncation points approach from inside the interval. Check every relevant side of every singularity.

derivation.text: Avoid zero initially.
A positive exponent makes the lower-end term vanish.
The threshold still diverges.

workedExamples.title: Do not cross an interior singularity
steps: The left integral is $\ln\delta\to-\infty$; the right is $-\ln\delta\to\infty$.
Neither converges, so cancellation is invalid.
workedExamples.answer: Divergent; a zero symmetric principal value is a different concept.

commonMistakes.claim: Every vertical asymptote implies infinite area.
commonMistakes.correction: $x^{-1/2}$ is unbounded at zero but has finite integral.

commonMistakes.claim: Just substitute the endpoints into an antiderivative.
commonMistakes.correction: Locate all singularities first. The fundamental theorem cannot be used across one.

practice.hint: Use a limit at the lower endpoint.
solution: $[\frac32x^{2/3}]_\delta^1\to\frac32$.

practice.hint: The issue is behavior near zero.
solution: $[-x^{-1}]_\delta^1=\delta^{-1}-1\to\infty$.

practice.hint: Integrate by parts, then take the lower-end limit.
solution: $[x\ln x-x]_\delta^1=-1-\delta\ln\delta+\delta$; $\delta\ln\delta\to0$.

practice.problem: An antiderivative difference for $\int_0^2\frac{dx}{(x-1)^2}$ is negative. What went wrong?
practice.answer: It crosses an interior singularity, invalidating the fundamental theorem.
solution: The integrand is positive on both sides, and both integrals tend to positive infinity near 1. It diverges.

learningCheck.question: For which exponents does $\int_0^1x^{-p}dx$ converge?
learningCheck.explanation: Near zero, the spike must be weak enough; this reverses the tail condition at infinity.

teaching.explain: Mark every unbounded point on the interval. The whole integral exists only if each required one-sided limit exists.

steps.title: An integrable spike
steps.instruction: Set the exponent to 0.5 and lower endpoint to 0.1.
steps.observation: The limiting total is 2, but the truncation still omits $2\sqrt{0.1}$.

steps.title: Approach zero
steps.instruction: Set the exponent to 0.5 and lower endpoint to 0.001.
steps.observation: The height grows, yet the omitted area shrinks.

steps.title: A nonintegrable spike
steps.instruction: Set the exponent to 1 and lower endpoint to 0.001.
steps.observation: The area is $-\ln0.001$, unbounded as the lower endpoint approaches zero.

interactiveVisual.caption: Truncate the spike of $[0,\delta)$ and display $\int_\delta^1x^{-p}dx$.
interactiveVisual.prediction: As the lower endpoint shrinks, which exponents keep the area finite?

objectives: Check every endpoint and interior singularity
Determine integrability of power spikes near zero
Recognize invalid use of the fundamental theorem across singularities

lessons.title: Surface area of revolution
lessons.subtitle: Circumference times a small arc length
lessons.concept: Rotating a small arc produces a narrow band, with area approximately circumference times arc length.
lessons.intuition: Volume uses disks; surface area uses circumferences. Their pieces and formulas differ.

body.title: Why include arc length?
body.text: A sloping arc is longer than its horizontal projection. Use $ds=\sqrt{1+(f\prime)^2}dx$, not simply $dx$.

body.title: Which radius?
body.text: The radius is distance to the axis. Around the horizontal line $y=c$, use $|f(x)-c|$.

body.title: Are end caps included?
body.text: This formula gives lateral area only. Add end caps separately for a closed surface. Retracing a curve counts the surface repeatedly.

formalDefinition.text: Circumference times a small arc length
conditions: $f$ is continuously differentiable on $[a,b]$, rotated about $y=c$, without repeated counting. Only lateral area is included.

derivation.text: Approximate each small arc by a segment.
Its rotation gives a narrow frustum band.
Refine the partition and take a limit.

workedExamples.title: A cone's lateral area
workedExamples.problem: Rotate $y=x$, $0\leq x\leq1$ about the horizontal axis. Find its lateral area.

workedExamples.title: A cylinder
workedExamples.problem: Rotate $y=2$, $0\leq x\leq3$ about the horizontal axis. Find its lateral area.
steps: The radius is 2; the arc-length element is $dx$.

commonMistakes.claim: Surface area still uses $\pi r^2$.
commonMistakes.correction: That is cross-sectional area. A lateral band uses $2\pi r\,ds$.

commonMistakes.claim: Lateral area automatically includes end caps.
commonMistakes.correction: End caps require separate calculation; the surface may not be capped at all.

practice.problem: Find the lateral area from rotating $y=3$, $0\leq x\leq2$ about the horizontal axis.
Find the lateral area from rotating $y=2x$, $0\leq x\leq1$ about the horizontal axis.
solution: $S=2\pi\int_0^1 2x\sqrt5 dx=2\pi\sqrt5$.

practice.problem: Find the lateral area from rotating $y=-1$, $0\leq x\leq2$ about the horizontal axis.
solution: The radius is $|y|=1$, and $S=2\pi\int_0^2dx=4\pi$.

practice.problem: What is the total area of a cylinder with radius $2$, length $3$, including both end caps?
practice.hint: Add two circles to the lateral area.
solution: The lateral area is $12\pi$; each cap has area $\pi\cdot2^2=4\pi$; total $20\pi$.

learningCheck.question: What is the small piece in a surface-of-revolution integral?
learningCheck.explanation: Circumference times arc length along the curve.

teaching.explain: For a surface, cut the generating curve into small arcs and rotate each into a narrow band.

steps.title: Gentle slope
steps.observation: The top radius is 0.5; the slant height is $\sqrt{1.25}$.

steps.title: Unit slope
steps.observation: The lateral area is $\pi\sqrt2$, excluding caps.

steps.title: Steep slope
steps.observation: The lateral area is $2\pi\sqrt5$; this is not volume.

interactiveVisual.prediction: As the slope increases, what happens to both radius and slant height?

Choose the correct radius and arc length
Distinguish lateral area, caps and volume

lessons.title: Mass, moments and center of mass
lessons.subtitle: Weight position by mass
lessons.concept: The center of mass is a mass-weighted average, not a simple average of boundary positions.
lessons.intuition: The midpoint works for equal masses. For a continuous distribution, sum mass times position and divide by total mass.

body.title: A thin rod
body.text: With linear density $\rho(x)$, $dm=\rho(x)dx$. Mass is $\int dm$; moment about the origin is $\int x\,dm$.

body.title: A planar lamina
body.text: A uniform lamina lies between $g(x)$ and $f(x)$. A vertical strip has area $(f-g)dx$ and midpoint height $\frac{f+g}{2}$.

body.title: What does symmetry simplify?
body.text: A symmetric mass distribution places the center of mass on the symmetry axis. Symmetric shape alone is insufficient if density is asymmetric.

formalDefinition.text: Weight position by mass
formalDefinition.latex: \bar x=\frac{\int x\,dm}{\int dm},\qquad\bar y=\frac{\int y\,dm}{\int dm}
conditions: Total mass is positive and finite; moments exist. Uniform-lamina formulas require constant area density.

derivation.text: Add the small masses.
Add each mass times its position.
Match the moment with a mass concentrated at the center of mass.

workedExamples.title: A rod heavier toward the right
workedExamples.problem: On $0\leq x\leq1$, density is $\rho(x)=2x$. Find the center of mass.

workedExamples.title: A triangular lamina
workedExamples.problem: Find the center of mass of the uniform lamina $0\leq y\leq x$, $0\leq x\leq1$.
steps: Moment about the vertical axis is $\int_0^1x^2dx=\frac13$; about the horizontal axis, $\frac12\int_0^1x^2dx=\frac16$.

commonMistakes.claim: The center of mass must be the geometric center.
commonMistakes.correction: Weight by mass. For a lamina with a hole, the center of mass can even lie outside the material.

commonMistakes.claim: Moment about the horizontal axis integrates horizontal position.
commonMistakes.correction: Distance to that axis is the vertical coordinate. Draw the moment arm first.

practice.problem: Mass 1 is at $x=0$ and mass 3 at $x=2$. Find the center of mass.
solution: $\bar x=\frac{1\cdot0+3\cdot2}{4}=\frac32$.

practice.problem: Find the center of mass of a uniform rod on $[2,6]$.
solution: Constant density puts it at the midpoint $\frac{2+6}{2}=4$.

practice.problem: On $[0,1]$, density is $\rho=3x^2$. Find the center of mass.
Find the center of mass of the uniform rectangle $0\leq x\leq2,0\leq y\leq4$.
solution: Symmetry about both midlines places it at their intersection.

learningCheck.question: If a rod is denser on the right, which way does its center of mass shift?
learningCheck.explanation: Mass elements on the right carry greater weight in the average.

teaching.explain: Each small piece contributes its position, weighted by its mass.

steps.title: A uniform rod
steps.observation: The center of mass is 0.5 and total mass is 1.

steps.title: Heavier on the right
steps.observation: Mass is 2; the center of mass is $\frac7{12}$.

steps.title: Increase the gradient
steps.observation: The center of mass is $\frac58$, still inside the rod.

interactiveVisual.caption: Vary density $\rho(x)=1+cx$ on $[0,1]$ and track the center of mass.
interactiveVisual.prediction: When the right side is heavier, does the center of mass stay at the midpoint?

Compute mass-weighted centers
Use symmetry of the mass distribution

lessons.title: Pressure and work by layers
lessons.subtitle: Depth and lifting distance vary with position
lessons.concept: Total force and work accumulate layer contributions; force or travel distance can differ between layers.
lessons.intuition: Water pressure increases with depth. Using one depth for an entire gate only works if it is the correct average.

body.title: Force on a gate
body.text: Hydrostatic gauge pressure is $\rho g h$. Strip area is width times thickness, so $dF=\rho g h\,dA$.

body.title: What changes for pumping work?
body.text: A layer weighs $\rho g\,dV$; multiply by its lift to the outlet: $dW=\rho g\ell\,dV$. Tank shape is specified by horizontal cross-sectional area $A(y)$, not base area alone. The water examples use $\rho=1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.

body.title: Why draw coordinates first?
body.text: Mark the surface, bottom, outlet and positive direction. Then express both depth and lift as functions of position.

formalDefinition.text: Depth and lifting distance vary with position
conditions: Water is at rest, with known density and gravity. Use gauge pressure, neglect flow losses and keep units consistent.

derivation.text: Depth is nearly constant across a thin horizontal strip.
Refine the strips to obtain total hydrostatic force.
Multiply each layer's weight by its lift to obtain work.

workedExamples.title: A rectangular gate
workedExamples.problem: A vertical gate has width $2\,\mathrm m$ and extends $3\,\mathrm m$ below the surface. With water density $1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$ and $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$, find the resultant force.

workedExamples.title: Pumping a cylindrical tank
workedExamples.problem: A vertical cylindrical tank has constant horizontal cross-sectional area $1\,\mathrm{m^2}$ and water depth $2\,\mathrm m$. Pump it empty to a fixed outlet $2\,\mathrm m$ above the bottom, neglecting losses. Find the work.
steps: Set the bottom at $y=0$. A layer has volume $1\,dy$, weight $9800\,dy$ and lifting distance $2-y$ to the fixed outlet.
$W=9800\int_0^2(2-y)\,dy=19600\,\mathrm J$. The water level falls; the outlet height stays fixed.

commonMistakes.claim: Total work equals total weight.
commonMistakes.correction: Multiply weight by distance too; each layer generally travels a different distance.

commonMistakes.claim: Pressure and resultant force are the same quantity.
commonMistakes.correction: Pressure is force per area. Integrate it over area to obtain force.

practice.problem: A rectangular gate has width $1\,\mathrm m$ and depth $2\,\mathrm m$ below the surface. Find the resultant force.

A vertical cylindrical tank has cross-sectional area $1\,\mathrm{m^2}$, water depth $2\,\mathrm m$ and a fixed outlet $3\,\mathrm m$ above its bottom. With $\rho=1000\,\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, $g=9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ and no losses, find the work to empty it.
practice.hint: Each layer travels one additional meter.

practice.problem: A spring has $k=20\,\mathrm{N/m}$. Find the work to stretch it from 0 to $0.5\,\mathrm m$.
Does bottom pressure times total area overestimate or underestimate force on a vertical gate?
practice.answer: Overestimate, for a nondegenerate vertical gate.
practice.hint: The bottom has the greatest depth.
solution: Every other point has lower pressure; replacing all pressures by the maximum overestimates the integral.

learningCheck.question: For pumping, what is one layer's work contribution?
learningCheck.explanation: Weight is the ideal lifting force; multiply by displacement to obtain work.

teaching.explain: First define a small layer's physical contribution, then sum. The integral follows the model.

steps.observation: Force per unit width is $4900\,\mathrm N$.

steps.title: Two meters deep
steps.observation: Force per unit width is $19600\,\mathrm N$, four times the previous value.

steps.title: Three meters deep
steps.observation: Force per unit width is $44100\,\mathrm N$; bottom pressure does not represent the whole gate.

interactiveVisual.prediction: If depth doubles, does force per unit width only double?

Set up work integrals with varying lift
Check directions, units and assumptions

lessons.title: Sequences and limits
lessons.subtitle: Track the index, not continuous time
lessons.concept: A sequence converges when every sufficiently late term stays close to one number. Finitely many initial terms do not determine its limit.
lessons.intuition: $a_n=\frac1n$ approaches zero without ever equaling it. Sequence indices are integers.

body.title: Making closeness precise
body.text: For every positive tolerance, there is an index beyond which all terms lie within that tolerance of the limit. A few close terms do not suffice.

body.title: Computing limits
body.text: Use limit laws, squeezing or a related continuous function. The quotient law requires a nonzero denominator limit.

body.title: Must oscillation diverge?
body.text: Oscillation can converge if its amplitude vanishes. $(-1)^n$ diverges, while $\frac{(-1)^n}{n}$ tends to zero.

formalDefinition.text: Track the index, not continuous time
conditions: The index $n$ is a positive integer. The threshold $N$ may depend on tolerance, not on the later term chosen.

derivation.text: Bound the reciprocal using the tolerance.
Choose a strictly larger integer threshold.
Every term beyond that threshold meets the tolerance.

workedExamples.title: A polynomial ratio
steps: Divide numerator and denominator by $n$, giving $\frac{3+1/n}{2-5/n}$.
The denominator tends to nonzero 2, so the quotient law applies.

workedExamples.title: Convergent oscillation
steps: The right side tends to zero; squeeze the sequence to zero.

commonMistakes.claim: One sufficiently close term proves convergence.
commonMistakes.correction: Every sufficiently late term must be close.

practice.answer: Its odd and even subsequences have different limits.
solution: Odd terms equal $-1$; even terms equal 1. Convergence would require the same limit for both.

solution: $n>100$, so every $n\geq101$ satisfies the requirement.
$\sqrt{n^2+n}-n=\frac{n}{\sqrt{n^2+n}+n}=\frac1{\sqrt{1+1/n}+1}\to\frac12$.

lessons.title: Monotone bounded sequences and recurrences
lessons.subtitle: Establish convergence before solving for a limit
lessons.concept: A bounded monotone real sequence converges. Pass a recurrence to its limit only after proving convergence.
lessons.intuition: A sequence rising beneath a ceiling approaches a height without necessarily reaching it in finitely many steps.

body.title: Which bound is needed?
body.text: An increasing sequence needs an upper bound; a decreasing one needs a lower bound. An unbounded monotone sequence may tend to infinity. The supremum is the least upper bound.

body.title: Finding a recursive limit
body.text: Use induction to establish an invariant interval and monotonicity. Then use continuity of the recurrence function to pass to the limit.

body.title: Is every fixed point a possible limit?
body.text: No. The initial value and invariant interval select branches; solving a fixed-point equation does not prove convergence.

formalDefinition.text: Establish convergence before solving for a limit
conditions: Use completeness of the real numbers, monotonicity and a finite bound in the appropriate direction.

derivation.text: Take the supremum as candidate limit.
Every smaller number fails to be an upper bound.
Monotonicity traps all later terms in a narrow band.

workedExamples.title: A square-root recurrence
steps: If $1\leq a_n<2$, the next term stays in the interval; also $\sqrt{2+x}>x$ holds for $1\leq x<2$.
Increasing and bounded above, it converges. The nonnegative solution of $L=\sqrt{2+L}$ is 2.

workedExamples.title: An averaging recurrence
steps: The error decays geometrically; the sequence increases without exceeding 3.

commonMistakes.claim: A recurrence with a fixed point must converge.
commonMistakes.correction: $a_{n+1}=-a_n$ has fixed point zero, but nonzero initial values oscillate.

commonMistakes.claim: Boundedness makes monotonicity unnecessary.
commonMistakes.correction: Bounded oscillation need not converge.

practice.problem: Is $a_n=1-\frac1n$ monotone and bounded? Find its limit.
practice.answer: Increasing, bounded above by 1, with limit 1.

practice.hint: Write the error relative to the fixed point.
solution: $4-a_{n+1}=\frac12(4-a_n)$, so the error tends to zero.

practice.problem: Can this theorem give a finite limit for the monotone sequence $a_n=n$?
practice.answer: No; an upper bound is missing.
solution: The sequence is strictly increasing and unbounded, so it tends to positive infinity.

practice.problem: Given $a_1=1,a_{n+1}=2-a_n$, if $a_1$ is changed to 0, is the limit still 1?
practice.answer: Starting at 1 gives the constant sequence 1; starting at 0 gives alternating 0 and 2.
practice.hint: A fixed point does not guarantee convergence.
solution: The first four terms reveal the cycle; the two subsequences have different limits.

choices: Assume convergence and accept all roots
Prove convergence using bounds and monotonicity
learningCheck.explanation: Passing to a limit requires a convergence argument first.

teaching.explain: A fixed-point equation identifies where a limit could be. Bounds and monotonicity establish that the sequence actually approaches one.

lessons.title: Infinite series and partial sums
lessons.subtitle: Define infinite addition through finite sums
lessons.concept: A series converges when its partial sums converge. Terms tending to zero are necessary, not sufficient.
lessons.intuition: Ever smaller contributions can still produce an unbounded total. $\frac1n$ is the key counterexample.

body.title: Sequence versus series
body.text: $a_n$ describes one contribution; $S_N$ describes the accumulated total. Their limits answer different questions.

body.title: What if terms do not tend to zero?
body.text: If partial sums have a finite limit, $a_n=S_n-S_{n-1}\to0$. Thus terms not tending to zero force divergence. The converse fails.

body.title: Can finitely many terms change convergence?
body.text: Adding or removing finitely many terms changes the sum but not convergence. The infinite tail decides.

formalDefinition.text: Define infinite addition through finite sums
conditions: Use the specified summation order. Convergence means a finite real limit.

derivation.text: Assume partial sums converge.
Their consecutive difference is one term.
Subtract limits to obtain the necessary condition.

workedExamples.title: Terms fail to vanish
steps: The necessary condition fails; no further partial-sum test is needed.

workedExamples.title: The harmonic series
workedExamples.problem: Why does $\sum\frac1n$ diverge although its terms vanish?
steps: Group terms by $[2^{k-1}+1,2^k]$; each group has $2^{k-1}$ terms.
Each term in a group is at least $\frac1{2^k}$; each group contributes at least $\frac12$, with arbitrarily many groups.
workedExamples.answer: Partial sums are unbounded; the series diverges.

commonMistakes.claim: $a_n\to0$ implies convergence of the series.
commonMistakes.correction: The harmonic series disproves this.

commonMistakes.claim: A divergent series must have terms tending to infinity.
commonMistakes.correction: Terms may tend to zero while the accumulated sum remains unbounded.

solution: Terms tend to 1, not zero.

practice.problem: What happens to the partial sums of $\sum_{n=1}^\infty(-1)^n$?
practice.answer: They oscillate between two values and do not converge.
practice.hint: Compute odd and even partial sums separately.

practice.problem: Increase the first term of a convergent series by 7. What changes?
practice.answer: It still converges; its sum increases by 7.
solution: Every partial sum increases by 7, so does the limit.

practice.problem: Given $a_n\to0$, what must you examine next to decide $\sum a_n$?
practice.answer: Examine partial sums or use an applicable convergence test.
practice.hint: A necessary condition is not sufficient.
solution: Vanishing terms exclude only the simplest cause of divergence. Geometric and harmonic tails behave differently.

learningCheck.question: What follows from $a_n\to0$?
learningCheck.explanation: This condition is necessary. The harmonic series shows it is insufficient.

teaching.explain: Track the entire running total, not just its newest contribution. Does that total approach a finite value?

lessons.title: Geometric and telescoping series
lessons.subtitle: One scales; the other cancels
lessons.concept: Find finite partial sums before taking a limit. Do not manipulate an infinite expression whose convergence is unknown.
lessons.intuition: Multiplying a geometric sum by its ratio shifts its terms. Telescoping expresses terms as differences so the interior cancels.

body.title: Why must the ratio have magnitude below one?
body.text: The finite-sum remainder contains $r^{N+1}$, which vanishes only when $|r|<1$. Treat $r=1$ separately; $r=-1$ oscillates.

body.title: Does the starting index matter?
body.text: Starting at power zero differs from starting at power one. Write the first two terms to avoid losing a ratio factor.

body.title: What survives telescoping?
body.text: Write the first and last terms explicitly. The surviving boundary terms determine convergence.

formalDefinition.text: One scales; the other cancels
conditions: The finite-sum formula requires $r\neq1$. If $a\neq0$, the infinite geometric series converges exactly when $|r|<1$.

derivation.text: Multiply the finite sum by its ratio and subtract.
Solve for the finite sum.
Within the convergence range, the tail vanishes.

workedExamples.title: Check the starting index
steps: The first term is $\frac13$; the ratio is $\frac13$.

commonMistakes.claim: Any ratio can enter the infinite-sum formula.
commonMistakes.correction: Check $|r|<1$ first.

commonMistakes.claim: Cancellation removes every term.
commonMistakes.correction: Retain the first and last boundary contributions.

solution: $|r|=\frac14<1$; the sum is $\frac1{1-1/4}=\frac43$.

practice.hint: A negative ratio can still converge.
solution: $|r|=\frac12<1$; the sum is $\frac1{1+1/2}=\frac23$.

practice.hint: The telescoping sum begins at the second term.
solution: $S_N=\frac12-\frac1{N+1}\to\frac12$.

practice.hint: Check the ratio range and positivity.
solution: The ratio's magnitude exceeds one and terms do not vanish; finite sums $2^{N+1}-1$ are unbounded.

learningCheck.question: What is the sum of $\sum_{n=1}^\infty r^n$ when $|r|<1$?
learningCheck.explanation: Starting at power one makes the first term the ratio itself.

teaching.explain: Perform each manipulation on a finite sum first. Keeping the uncancelled tail prevents assigning a false finite value to divergence.

lessons.title: The integral test and tail bounds
lessons.subtitle: Trap a positive tail between areas
lessons.concept: A positive, continuous, decreasing function links an integral to a series and bounds the tail after a finite partial sum.
lessons.intuition: Unit-width rectangles on opposite sides of a decreasing curve bound its area. Two integrals trap the tail sum.

body.title: Essential hypotheses
body.text: The function is eventually positive, continuous and decreasing, and its integer values give the terms. Handle any finite initial segment separately.

body.title: Does the integral equal the series sum?
body.text: Usually not. They share convergence behavior; tail integrals provide bounds, not equality.

body.title: Choosing the number of terms
body.text: If the upper tail bound is below the tolerance, the partial sum meets the error target. The benchmark $\sum_{n=1}^\infty n^{-p}$ is a $p$-series and converges exactly when $p>1$.

formalDefinition.text: Trap a positive tail between areas
conditions: $f$ is positive, continuous and decreasing on $[N,\infty)$, and its improper integral converges.

derivation.text: Use monotonicity to compare each rectangle with neighboring areas.
Sum from the first omitted term.
Let the upper endpoint tend to infinity to bound the tail.

workedExamples.title: A reciprocal-square tail
workedExamples.problem: Bound the error after 10 terms of $\sum\frac1{n^2}$.
steps: The function is positive, continuous and decreasing; its tail integral is simple.

workedExamples.title: A logarithmic boundary
steps: Its associated function is positive and decreasing on $x\geq2$.
Set $u=\ln x$; the integral is the finite value $\int_{\ln2}^\infty u^{-2}du$.

commonMistakes.claim: Any function representation permits the integral test.
commonMistakes.correction: Check positivity, continuity and eventual decrease.

commonMistakes.claim: The sum equals the integral starting at one.
commonMistakes.correction: Rectangles differ from the curve. The test gives convergence equivalence and tail bounds.

solution: $\int_1^\infty x^{-p}dx$ converges exactly when $p>1$; for $p\leq0$, the term test also applies.

practice.problem: For reciprocal squares with bound $R_N\le1/N$, how many terms guarantee this bound is at most $0.01$?
solution: $R_N\leq\frac1N$; choose $N=100$.
$\int_2^R\frac{dx}{x\ln x}=\ln\ln R-\ln\ln2\to\infty$.

practice.problem: For $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}1/n^3$, use $\int_{10}^{\infty}x^{-3}\,dx$ to bound the tail after 10 terms. What is the bound?
solution: $R_{10}\leq\int_{10}^\infty x^{-3}dx=\frac1{2\cdot10^2}$.

learningCheck.question: What does the integral test generally provide?
choices: Convergence equivalence and applicable tail bounds
The sum of any signed series
learningCheck.explanation: Positive decreasing curves and rectangles trap tails; they usually do not coincide.

teaching.explain: Replace an infinite unseen tail by two computable areas, obtaining both convergence and a useful error range.

lessons.title: Comparison and limit comparison
lessons.subtitle: Match an unfamiliar tail to a known one
lessons.concept: Compare positive terms with a known series. Limit comparison checks whether their tails differ by a finite positive factor.
lessons.intuition: For large $n$, $\frac1{n^2+1}$ behaves like $\frac1{n^2}$. Limit comparison turns this resemblance into a precise ratio.

body.title: Which direction works?
body.text: Below a convergent positive series implies convergence; above a divergent one implies divergence. Reversing either comparison is inconclusive.

body.title: Limit-comparison hypotheses
body.text: Both sequences must eventually be positive and their ratio must tend to a finite positive number. Limits zero or infinity can support one-sided conclusions, not automatic equivalence.

body.title: Choosing a reference
body.text: For rational terms, compare leading powers; for radicals, compare growth rates. Initial inequalities do not determine tail behavior.

formalDefinition.text: Match an unfamiliar tail to a known one
formalDefinition.latex: a_n,b_n>0,\quad\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{b_n}=c\in(0,\infty)\ \Longrightarrow\ \sum a_n,\sum b_n\text{ converge or diverge together}
conditions: Terms are eventually positive; finitely many initial terms do not affect convergence.

derivation.text: A positive ratio limit traps the terms between two positive multiples.
If the reference converges, use an upper comparison.
If the reference diverges, use a lower comparison.

workedExamples.title: Direct comparison
steps: Reciprocal squares converge, so the smaller positive series converges.

workedExamples.title: Limit comparison
steps: The harmonic series diverges, and the ratio limit is finite and positive.

commonMistakes.claim: Anything below a divergent series converges.
commonMistakes.correction: A divergent upper bound is too loose to decide.

commonMistakes.claim: A ratio tending to zero still guarantees the same behavior.
commonMistakes.correction: Zero does not guarantee equivalence; compare reciprocal squares with harmonic terms.

solution: Positive terms are at most $\frac1{n^2}$; the upper series converges.

practice.hint: Use limit comparison with harmonic terms.
solution: $\frac{n}{\sqrt{n^2+1}}\to1$, so it shares harmonic divergence.

practice.hint: Try two sequences satisfying the upper bound.
solution: $a_n=\frac1{n^2}$ converges, but $a_n=\frac1n$ diverges.
$\frac{(n+1)n^2}{n^3+2}\to1$; the finite positive ratio gives convergence.

learningCheck.question: Which comparison establishes convergence of a positive series?
learningCheck.explanation: The tails are bounded above by a finite total.

teaching.explain: Decide whether you need an upper or lower bound before choosing the reference.

lessons.title: Ratio and root tests
lessons.subtitle: Look for eventual geometric decay
lessons.concept: A limiting consecutive ratio or nth root below one gives a convergent geometric bound. A limit equal to one is inconclusive.
lessons.intuition: Factorials and exponentials often suit the ratio test; an overall $n$th power often suits the root test. Both seek a hidden geometric tail.

body.title: The ratio test
body.text: For eventually nonzero terms, compute the limit of $|a_{n+1}/a_n|$. Below one gives absolute convergence; above one or infinity gives divergence. Factorials satisfy $n!=1\cdot2\cdots n$, with $0!=1$.

body.title: The root test
body.text: Compute the limit of $\sqrt[n]{|a_n|}$, with the same threshold one. If the limit fails to exist, this limit version cannot be applied directly.

body.title: What if the limit is one?
body.text: Use another test. Both $\sum\frac1n$ and $\sum\frac1{n^2}$ have ratio limit one, but opposite convergence behavior.

formalDefinition.text: Look for eventual geometric decay
conditions: The chosen limit exists, possibly as positive infinity; ratio denominators are eventually nonzero. $L=1$ is inconclusive.

derivation.text: For a limit below one, choose an intermediate geometric ratio.
All sufficiently late ratios are at most that value.
The geometric tail converges, proving absolute convergence by comparison.

workedExamples.title: Factorials dominate exponentials
steps: The limit is below one, giving absolute convergence, not the sum.

workedExamples.title: An overall power
steps: Large initial terms do not change tail convergence.

commonMistakes.claim: A ratio tending to one implies divergence.
commonMistakes.correction: One is inconclusive; use another test.

commonMistakes.claim: The ratio test computes the sum.
commonMistakes.correction: It decides convergence, not the sum itself.

solution: The ratio is $\frac3{n+1}\to0$.
The ratio is $\frac{n+1}{2}\to\infty$; terms also fail to tend to zero.
The root is $\frac{n}{2n+1}\to\frac12<1$.

practice.problem: The ratio limit of $\sum\frac1{n^2}$ is one. What next?
practice.answer: Use the positive $p$-series result or integral test to establish convergence.
practice.hint: This is a familiar positive power tail.
solution: The ratio test is inconclusive; the $p$-series has $p=2>1$, so it converges.

learningCheck.question: A ratio limit equal to one means what?
learningCheck.explanation: Use comparison, integration or another applicable test.

teaching.explain: Below one, the tail eventually shrinks at least at some fixed geometric rate. One gives no such guarantee.

steps.observation: Terms may increase initially; the first few terms do not decide.

lessons.title: Alternating series and error
lessons.subtitle: Alternating decreasing terms trap the remainder
lessons.concept: Eventually nonincreasing positive magnitudes tending to zero give convergence. The next-term bound applies only after the truncation enters that decreasing tail.
lessons.intuition: Pair decreasing positive and negative terms: partial sums trap the limit from opposite sides. Keep an irregular initial segment before bounding its tail.

body.title: The two conditions
body.text: Magnitudes are eventually nonincreasing and tend to zero. Alternation alone is insufficient; a finite initial segment does not affect convergence.

body.title: What is the error's sign?
body.text: If $b_n$ decreases to zero from $n=n_0$, then for $N+1\ge n_0$, the remainder has the first omitted term's sign or is zero, with magnitude at most $b_{N+1}$. Do not apply the bound before decrease begins.

body.title: Does this bound work without alternation?
body.text: No. Positive tails can accumulate many terms and need integral, geometric or other estimates.

formalDefinition.text: Alternating decreasing terms trap the remainder
conditions: $b_n\ge0$; there exists $n_0$ such that $b_n$ is nonincreasing for $n\ge n_0$ and tends to zero. The error formula requires $N+1\ge n_0$.

derivation.text: Pair terms when decrease starts immediately. For eventual decrease, remove the finite initial segment and apply the same proof to the tail.
Odd partial sums decrease, even partial sums increase, and both trap the limit.
Their gap vanishes, yielding the next-term error bound.

workedExamples.title: The alternating harmonic series
workedExamples.problem: Using 100 terms for $1-\frac12+\frac13-\cdots$, what is the maximum error?
steps: The next magnitude is $\frac1{101}$ and its sign is positive, so the true sum is above the partial sum.

workedExamples.title: Choosing a count
workedExamples.problem: How many terms suffice to approximate $\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n^2}$ with error at most $0.001$?

commonMistakes.claim: Alternation alone guarantees convergence.
commonMistakes.correction: The magnitudes in $1-1+1-1+\cdots$ do not vanish; partial sums oscillate.

commonMistakes.claim: An error below the last term means the answer is exact.
commonMistakes.correction: Finite truncation remains approximate. Use the next term to bound its error.

practice.problem: What is the remainder's sign after 9 alternating harmonic terms?
solution: The tenth term is $-\frac1{10}$; the remainder is nonpositive, so the sum is at most the ninth partial sum.

practice.problem: Bound the error after 99 alternating harmonic terms.

solution: Magnitudes tend to 1, so terms do not vanish; the alternating-series test cannot establish convergence.
$n^{-1/2}$ is positive and decreases to zero, so the alternating series converges.

practice.problem: Let $b_1=1,b_2=100$, with $b_n=1/n$ when $n\ge3$. Does the alternating series converge? At $N=0$, can you use $|S|\le b_1$?
practice.answer: It converges, but the tail bound cannot be used before the decreasing portion begins.
practice.hint: Convergence concerns the eventual tail; an error bound also depends on where truncation occurs.
solution: Magnitudes decrease to zero from the third term, so the series converges.
The tail starting at the third term lies between $0$ and $1/3$; hence $-99\le S\le-99+1/3$, and clearly $|S|>1=b_1$.
In this example the next-term bound applies directly only for $N\ge2$.

learningCheck.explanation: Alternation and decreasing magnitudes together trap the tail.

lessons.title: Absolute and conditional convergence
lessons.subtitle: Remove signs and test the total magnitude
lessons.concept: Absolute convergence means the absolute-value series converges. Conditional convergence means the original series converges but its absolute-value series diverges.
lessons.intuition: Conditional convergence relies on cancellation; rearrangement can change the sum. Absolutely convergent sums are stable under rearrangement.

body.title: Why is absolute convergence stronger?
body.text: The magnitude of an original tail is at most its absolute-value tail. Making the latter small controls the former.

body.title: Classifying a series
body.text: Test absolute values first. If they converge, you are done. If they diverge, test the signed original instead of immediately declaring divergence.

body.title: Can terms be rearranged freely?
body.text: Finite sums can. Infinite sums need conditions: absolute convergence allows rearrangement; for conditional convergence retain the specified order.

formalDefinition.text: Remove signs and test the total magnitude
formalDefinition.latex: \sum|a_n|<\infty\Rightarrow\sum a_n\text{ converges};\qquad \sum a_n\text{ converges and }\sum|a_n|=\infty\Rightarrow\text{conditional convergence}
conditions: These are real series. Rearrangement invariance does not make arbitrary finite truncations equal.

derivation.text: Apply the triangle inequality to a finite tail.
Absolute convergence makes the bound arbitrarily small.
The original series satisfies the Cauchy criterion and converges.

workedExamples.title: Conditional convergence
steps: Its absolute-value series is harmonic and diverges.

workedExamples.title: Absolute convergence
steps: Its absolute-value series is the reciprocal-square series.
The power is 2, greater than 1, so the absolute sum is finite.

commonMistakes.correction: Conditional convergence is still possible; test the original series next.

commonMistakes.claim: Rearrangement cannot change any infinite sum.
commonMistakes.correction: A conditionally convergent sum can depend on order.

solution: Its absolute-value series is a convergent power tail with exponent 3.

solution: Magnitudes decrease to zero, so the original converges. The absolute-value power is $\frac12\leq1$, giving divergence.

solution: The magnitude $\frac{2^n}{n}$ does not vanish, violating the necessary condition.
$|\frac{\sin n}{n^2}|\leq\frac1{n^2}$; comparison gives absolute convergence.

learningCheck.explanation: Either conditional convergence or divergence is possible.

teaching.explain: First ask whether the total magnitude is finite without cancellation. If so, convergence is absolute; if convergence requires cancellation, it is conditional.

lessons.title: Power series and convergence intervals
lessons.subtitle: Treat each input as a separate series
lessons.concept: A power series converges inside its radius and diverges outside. Test each boundary point separately.
lessons.intuition: On $|x|<1$, $\sum x^n$ represents $\frac1{1-x}$. Outside this range, that series representation is invalid.

body.title: Center and radius
body.text: The center of $\sum c_n(x-a)^n$ is $a$. The radius measures distance from it and may be zero, positive finite or infinite.

body.title: Why are endpoints special?
body.text: The ratio test usually gives a strict inequality. At endpoints, harmonic, alternating harmonic or other series can arise, with different results on each side.

body.title: Does a defined function value imply a convergent expansion?
body.text: No. $\frac1{1-x}$ is defined at $x=2$, but its geometric expansion centered at zero diverges there.

formalDefinition.text: Treat each input as a separate series
conditions: Test endpoints $x=a\pm R$ separately. For $R=0$ only the center converges; for $R=\infty$ every input converges.

lessons.title: Differentiating and integrating power series
lessons.subtitle: Operate term by term inside the convergence radius
lessons.concept: Inside the convergence interval, power series can be differentiated and integrated term by term. The radius stays the same; endpoints may change.
lessons.intuition: Integrating a geometric series gives a logarithm; differentiating it gives another rational-function expansion.

body.title: Why emphasize the interior?
body.text: Arbitrary function series cannot be differentiated term by term. A power series and its derivative series converge uniformly on every closed interval strictly inside the radius, justifying differentiation. Uniform convergence of the original justifies integration. One term count controls all inputs in that interval at once.

body.title: Determining the integration constant
body.text: Integrate from the center or use a known function value to determine the constant. Do not lose the constant term.

body.title: What happens at endpoints?
body.text: Integration may gain endpoint convergence; differentiation may lose it. Substitute the endpoints again.

formalDefinition.text: Operate term by term inside the convergence radius
conditions: The original radius is $R>0$. Termwise integration is initially guaranteed only on the open interval; check boundaries separately.

derivation.text: Start with a convergent geometric series.
Integrate term by term from the center to the input.

lessons.title: Taylor polynomials
lessons.subtitle: Match a function's derivatives at one point
lessons.concept: A Taylor polynomial matches the value and first few derivatives at its center. This local agreement does not guarantee accuracy far away.
lessons.intuition: The linear term matches slope; the quadratic term matches curvature. Higher terms match higher derivatives, with factorials cancelling differentiation factors.

body.title: Why divide by a factorial?
body.text: The $k$th derivative of $c_k(x-a)^k$ at the center leaves $k!c_k$. Divide by $k!$ to match the corresponding derivative of the function.

body.title: Is Maclaurin a different method?
body.text: It is simply Taylor expansion centered at zero, with the same formula and reasoning.

body.title: Polynomial versus infinite series
body.text: A finite Taylor polynomial exists when the required derivatives exist. Equality with the infinite series additionally requires the remainder to vanish.

formalDefinition.text: Match a function's derivatives at one point
conditions: $f$ has derivatives through order $m$ at the center. Estimate the remainder separately to establish accuracy.

derivation.text: Write a candidate polynomial.

lessons.subtitle: Pair every approximation with an applicable bound
lessons.concept: A Taylor polynomial gives an approximation; a bound on the next derivative limits its error.
lessons.intuition: Closer to the center, $(x-a)^{m+1}$ is smaller. Derivatives may be large, so distance alone is insufficient.

body.title: Where must the derivative be bounded?
body.text: Throughout the interval from center to target, not just at the center.

body.title: Choosing the order
body.text: Bound the derivative on the interval, then require the remainder bound below tolerance. The derivative bound may change with order.

body.title: Does infinite smoothness guarantee equality with the series?
body.text: No. Define $f(x)=e^{-1/x^2}$ away from zero and $f(0)=0$. Every derivative at zero vanishes, but the function is positive elsewhere. Its Taylor series does not represent it. Away from zero, each derivative is a polynomial in $x^{-1}$ times $e^{-1/x^2}$. Exponential decay beats every negative power, allowing continuous extension of every derivative by zero.

formalDefinition.text: Pair every approximation with an applicable bound
conditions: $f$ has a continuous derivative of order $m+1$ on an interval containing $a,x$. The point $\xi$ lies between the endpoints, and $M$ bounds that derivative throughout.

derivation.text: The remainder is the function minus its matching polynomial.
Taylor's theorem expresses it using a higher derivative at an intermediate point.
Take absolute values and use a uniform derivative bound.

lessons.concept: Exponential, sine, cosine, geometric and logarithmic expansions generate many others by substitution and calculus. Keep each convergence range.

body.title: Which work everywhere?
body.text: The exponential, sine and cosine Maclaurin series converge to their functions at every finite real input, as vanishing remainders show.

body.title: Which have boundaries?
body.text: The geometric series works on $|x|<1$; logarithm $\ln(1+x)$ on $-1<x\leq1$; arctangent on $[-1,1]$. Endpoint identification for logarithm and arctangent needs a remainder argument or Abel's continuity theorem, not interior termwise integration alone.

body.title: Substituting inputs
body.text: Replace the entire input and transform the range too. For example, the zero-centered expansion of $\ln(1+x^2)$ works on $|x|\leq1$.

formalDefinition.text: Build from a few basic expansions
conditions: The first two formulas hold for all real inputs; the logarithmic formula requires $-1<x\leq1$. Cosine is $\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n}}{(2n)!}$, for all real inputs.

body.title: Bounding the approximation

body.title: How far should you expand?

lessons.title: The generalized binomial series
lessons.subtitle: Expand noninteger powers locally
lessons.concept: Binomial coefficients extend to any real exponent. Nonnegative integer exponents terminate; others generally yield infinite series with limited convergence ranges.
lessons.intuition: Square roots can be approximated by polynomial terms, but this expansion works only near its center.

body.title: Defining the coefficients
body.text: Multiply descending factors from the exponent, then divide by a factorial. The zeroth coefficient is one; no fractional or negative factorial is needed.

body.title: The valid range
body.text: For any real exponent, the series represents $(1+x)^\alpha$ on $|x|<1$; check endpoints separately. For a nonnegative integer, the finite polynomial identity has no radius restriction.

body.title: Checking an approximation
body.text: At the center, check the constant and derivative coefficients. For guaranteed accuracy, use a Taylor remainder rather than merely small terms.

formalDefinition.text: Expand noninteger powers locally
conditions: $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, $|x|<1$. For a nonnegative integer, termination gives a polynomial identity valid for all real inputs.

derivation.text: Compute derivatives of the power function at zero.

lessons.title: Parametric equations and motion
lessons.subtitle: Use one parameter to determine both coordinates
lessons.concept: Parametric equations specify how a point moves. The same geometric curve can have different directions and speeds.
lessons.intuition: $x=\cos t,y=\sin t$ describes a circle and also its starting point, direction and traversal time.

body.title: Is eliminating the parameter enough?
body.text: It reveals a geometric equation but loses direction, start, range and repeated tracing. State the parameter interval too.

body.title: Must the parameter be time?
body.text: It may be time, angle or another quantity. Derivatives have velocity units only if it represents time.

body.title: What does negative velocity mean?
body.text: A coordinate derivative may be negative, indicating motion against that axis. Speed is the nonnegative length of the velocity vector.

formalDefinition.text: Use one parameter to determine both coordinates
conditions: Coordinate functions are differentiable on the interval. Interpret units according to the parameter.

derivation.text: Describe a circle point with two coordinates.
Square and add to identify the geometric locus.
Derivatives retain the motion information.

workedExamples.problem: For $x=2\cos t,y=\sin t$, $0\leq t\leq2\pi$, describe the path and direction.

workedExamples.answer: An ellipse with horizontal semiaxis 2 and vertical semiaxis 1, traversed counterclockwise.

commonMistakes.correction: Direction, speed and repetition may all differ.

lessons.title: Tangents and arc length of parametric curves
lessons.subtitle: Differentiate with respect to the parameter first
lessons.concept: Parametric slope is vertical rate divided by horizontal rate. Arc length accumulates speed.
lessons.intuition: Over a short time, displacement has components $dx$ and $dy$. Slope uses their ratio; distance uses their Pythagorean length.

body.title: What if the horizontal derivative is zero?
body.text: A nonzero vertical derivative gives a vertical tangent. If both vanish, analyze the local path separately; the quotient formula fails.

body.title: Computing the second derivative
body.text: Differentiate the slope with respect to the parameter, then divide by $x\prime(t)$. The parameter derivative alone is not enough.

body.title: Can arc length count repetitions?
body.text: If the path retraces a segment, the integral measures total travel. To measure the geometric curve once, choose a nonrepeating interval.

body.title: Area in parametric form
body.text: Replace $dx$ by $x\prime(t)dt$: $\int y\,dx=\int y(t)x\prime(t)dt$. Increasing horizontal coordinate and nonnegative height give area beneath the curve. Reverse direction when the horizontal coordinate decreases; split at reversals and sign changes. Signed accumulation is not automatically geometric area.

formalDefinition.text: Differentiate with respect to the parameter first
conditions: Slope and second-derivative formulas require $x\prime(t)\neq0$ and sufficient smoothness. Arc length requires piecewise continuous differentiability; check repeated tracing.

lessons.title: Polar coordinates and curves
lessons.subtitle: Locate points using radius and direction
lessons.concept: Polar coordinates give radius and angle. A negative radius moves opposite the stated direction.
lessons.intuition: One point has many polar representations. Different coordinate pairs need not represent different points.

body.title: Converting to Cartesian coordinates
body.text: $x=r\cos\theta,y=r\sin\theta$. Distance from the origin is $|r|$, not always the signed $r$.

body.title: Finding intersections
body.text: Equal radii at the same angle find some intersections. Also check negative-radius representations and the origin: a point can have different angles.

formalDefinition.text: Locate points using radius and direction
conditions: Use radians. Any angle represents the origin when radius is zero. Recover angles using the correct quadrant.

lessons.title: Polar area and arc length
lessons.subtitle: Area uses sectors; length uses speed
lessons.concept: Polar area accumulates small sectors, while arc length accumulates short arcs. Check tracing ranges to avoid repetition.
lessons.intuition: A small sector has area about $\frac12r^2\Delta\theta$. Changing radius contributes to length, so the length formula includes both radius and its derivative.

body.title: Why the factor one-half?
body.text: Allocate a circle's area in proportion to the sector angle: $\pi r^2\cdot\frac{\Delta\theta}{2\pi}$.

body.text: Insert $x=r\cos\theta,y=r\sin\theta$ into parametric arc length; cross terms cancel after squaring and adding.

formalDefinition.text: Area uses sectors; length uses speed
conditions: The area formula describes a radial region covered once, usually with continuous nonnegative radius. Arc length requires piecewise continuous differentiability. Retracing counts again.

lessons.title: Differential equations and direction fields
lessons.subtitle: Find curves that follow a prescribed slope
lessons.concept: A differential equation specifies slope; an initial value specifies a starting point. A direction field shows the local directions allowed.
lessons.intuition: The unknown is a function. $y\prime=y$ asks for all curves whose rate equals their value; an initial value selects one.

body.title: Checking a solution

body.title: What does a direction field show?
body.text: At each $(x,y)$, draw a segment with slope $f(x,y)$. It suggests growth, decline and equilibria; finitely many segments do not prove existence.

body.title: Is the solution unique?
body.text: A continuous right side gives local existence. If its derivative with respect to the vertical variable is also continuous near the initial point, local uniqueness follows. Continuity alone need not give uniqueness.

formalDefinition.text: Find curves that follow a prescribed slope
conditions: One sufficient local-uniqueness condition is continuity of $f$ and $\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ near the initial point. The latter means differentiating in $y$ while holding $x$ fixed.

lessons.title: Separable equations
lessons.subtitle: Keep solutions that division might remove
lessons.concept: If a rate factors into a function of each variable, separate and integrate. Find equilibria before dividing by the dependent-variable factor.

body.title: Separating variables
body.text: On an interval with $g(y)\neq0$, rewrite $y\prime=f(x)g(y)$ as $\frac1{g(y)}dy=f(x)dx$, then integrate.

body.title: Keeping equilibrium solutions

formalDefinition.text: Keep solutions that division might remove

lessons.title: First-order linear equations
lessons.subtitle: Turn the left side into a product derivative
lessons.concept: For $y\prime+p(x)y=q(x)$, multiply by a suitable function to combine the left side into one product derivative.
lessons.intuition: Design a factor that supplies the missing term in the product rule, rather than guessing a solution.

body.title: Deriving the integrating factor
body.text: We want $\mu y\prime+\mu p y=(\mu y)\prime$, requiring $\mu\prime=\mu p$; choose $\mu=e^{\int p dx}$.

body.title: Why omit its multiplicative constant?
body.text: Any nonzero constant scales the whole equation equally and is absorbed into the solution's constant.

body.title: What makes an equation linear?
body.text: The unknown and its derivative appear to the first power, with coefficients depending only on the independent variable. Terms $y^2$ or $yy\prime$ do not fit.

formalDefinition.text: Turn the left side into a product derivative
conditions: $p,q$ are continuous on the interval. Normalize the derivative coefficient to one; the integrating factor is nonzero there.

derivation.text: Apply the product rule to identify the condition.
Choose a factor satisfying it.
Integrate and divide by the nonzero factor.

lessons.title: Euler's method and the logistic model
lessons.subtitle: Step along the current slope and examine equilibria
lessons.concept: Euler advances using the current slope. Logistic growth slows as remaining capacity decreases.
lessons.intuition: A stable continuous model can have unreasonable numerical behavior at large step sizes. Separate model properties from algorithm properties.

body.title: One Euler step
body.text: At $(x_n,y_n)$, use slope $f(x_n,y_n)$ over width $h$. Recompute slope every step rather than following the initial tangent forever.

body.title: Logistic equilibria
body.text: $y\prime=ry(1-y/K)$, $r,K>0$. Equilibria are zero and $K$. Positive solutions grow below $K$ and fall above $K$.

body.title: Understanding numerical error
body.text: On a fixed finite interval, if the exact solution has bounded second derivative and the right side has bounded vertical derivative near it, Euler's global error is bounded by a constant times step size. Halving steps typically reduces error, but a few comparisons do not establish a uniform guarantee.

formalDefinition.text: Step along the current slope and examine equilibria
conditions: Euler uses a fixed positive step size. Convergence requires sufficient regularity and controlled derivatives on the interval. For logistic $r,K>0$ and positive initial values, compare with an explicit solution.

derivation.text: Separate the logistic equation, keeping both equilibria.
Use partial fractions and solve for positive initial values.
Approximate one step using the current slope.

commonMistakes.correction: It is discrete approximation; compare it with exact solutions or error bounds.

commonMistakes.claim: A stable continuous model stays stable at every step size.
commonMistakes.correction: Large steps may cause oscillation, overshoot or unrealistic negative values.
